segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: I think we all have people in our lives who we love, but there's no talking to them. They have their way of seeing things or doing things, and it's hard to take. And no matter how you try to talk it out, it goes nowhere. It doesn't get solved, even if they also want things to change.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: We're devoting our entire show today to a story like that from Zach Mack, who's a reporter. And the story is about him and his dad and how they both wanted to mend a rift that had grown between them that had lasted for years, but they couldn't figure out how until Zach's dad offered a very surprising way out.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: That's going to be our whole show today-- his dad's unusual solution and how it played out. That's all I'm going to say for now. From WBEZ Chicago, it's This American Life. I'm Ira Glass. And with that, I turn things over to Zach.

segments.speaker: Zach Mack
segments.text: This all started about a year ago. My father called and left me this message.

segments.speaker: Dad
segments.text: Hey, Zach. Dad again. Good conversation last week-- last night. Hey, I didn't remember to tell you this because I was kind of tired. But they're going to shut us down again. And it's going to be a worse shutdown than 2020 because of this EMP, that all the supply lines are going to be disrupted.

segments.speaker: Dad
segments.text: So you really want to store up two months' worth of food and water because they probably won't be able to pump water throughout the city, because that's all controlled by computers and electronics. And the EMP is going to shut down everything electronic.

segments.speaker: Zach Mack
segments.text: My dad's talking about something called an ElectroMagnetic Pulse, EMP for short, which I only know about because it's what George Clooney uses in the movie Ocean's Eleven to pull off the casino heist.

segments.speaker: Danny
segments.text: What's a pinch?

segments.speaker: Basher
segments.text: A pinch is a device which creates like a cardiac arrest for any broadband electrical circuitry-- an electromagnetic pulse which shuts down any power source within its blast radius.

segments.speaker: Dad
segments.text: You should buy enough water.

segments.speaker: Zach Mack
segments.text: I can't remember a single other time Dad left me a message expressing a safety concern, but he was really convinced this was going to happen. At one point, he even did a little math for how much water I would need to survive.

segments.speaker: Dad
segments.text: So I would buy 60 times 10, which is 600 ounces. I know. I know it sounds like conspiracy theory, but they're going to do this. This is what they're planning. And I just want to have you be prepared. OK?

segments.speaker: Zach Mack
segments.text: OK, so just a little background-- I wouldn't describe my father as a paranoid person. I wouldn't even call him an anxious person. He's actually an optimist and usually prefers to keep things light, so a lot of dad jokes.

segments.speaker: Zach Mack
segments.text: What else? He's held down the same job forever. He has friends-- not close ones, but there's dudes he goes skiing and sailing with. When I was growing up, Dad was kind of in his own world. Mom was always the more involved parent, the one who knew all my friends and whatever was going on with me.

segments.speaker: Zach Mack
segments.text: Dad and I have never been particularly close. Typically, when I hear from him on the phone, it's during an Ohio State football game. We both love the Buckeyes, so during a game, he'll call me, like, five or six times, but not much beyond games, though. Ohio State football is the one thing we can agree on.

segments.speaker: Zach Mack
segments.text: The thing we can't seem to agree on is reality. Like so many people, Dad's gotten swept up in conspiracies. Lately, he's been talking about chemtrails, that the government can control the weather, that January 6 was staged by what he calls the "deep state."

segments.speaker: Zach Mack
segments.text: As he's gotten more extreme in the last few years, I've seen my mom and sister retract and shut down around him. I'm typically the one who challenges Dad on this stuff. Because I'm a reporter, I can't resist taking the bait.

segments.speaker: Dad
segments.text: It's called denying us freedom of speech.

segments.speaker: Zach Mack
segments.text: No, no.

segments.speaker: Dad
segments.text: It's called denying us freedom of speech.

segments.speaker: Zach Mack
segments.text: It's misinformation.

segments.speaker: Dad
segments.text: No. Who gets the right to label it misinformation?

segments.speaker: Zach Mack
segments.text: Of course, it never goes anywhere, until a year ago. After a family blowout over the holidays that was so bad, my sister and I left early, I decided to confront my father. I could see how his beliefs were starting to strain the family, and I worried that pretty soon, there may be no coming back for him. I told him I thought he was being radicalized online and pleaded with him to hear me.

segments.speaker: Zach Mack
segments.text: As always, he didn't agree. But what he did next surprised me. Dad texted me a photo of a sheet of paper where, in his barely legible cursive, he had written out a list of 10 predictions, 10 things that he was positive would all take place sometime in 2024, assuring me that when all of these things happened, I would see once and for all that he was right. At the bottom of the page was a challenge to a bet for $10,000.

segments.speaker: Zach Mack
segments.text: And let me just say, Dad and I are not big gamblers, nor are we rich. 10k is easily more money than either of us has ever wagered. Looking over the list, I was a combination of surprised, horrified, and also, it was a little hard to take seriously. I immediately called him up to discuss the terms of the bet.

segments.speaker: Zach Mack
segments.text: Do you have the list in front of you? Because you--

segments.speaker: Dad
segments.text: Yeah, yeah.

segments.speaker: Zach Mack
segments.text: Can you walk me through the 1 through 10? I just want to add-- each one, I'll probably have a couple clarifying questions.

segments.speaker: Dad
segments.text: Yeah, absolutely.

segments.speaker: Zach Mack
segments.text: Keep in mind, this call took place back in January 2024.

segments.speaker: Dad
segments.text: Number one, Obama will be found guilty of treason in 2024.

segments.speaker: Zach Mack
segments.text: So, like, by a court?

segments.speaker: Dad
segments.text: Yes.

segments.speaker: Zach Mack
segments.text: OK. Not the court of public opinion?

segments.speaker: Dad
segments.text: Correct.

segments.speaker: Zach Mack
segments.text: OK. And then number two?

segments.speaker: Dad
segments.text: Oh, yeah. Biden will be found guilty of treason in 2024.

segments.speaker: Zach Mack
segments.text: Just treason for something specific?

segments.speaker: Dad
segments.text: For selling all those secrets that he had in the back of his Corvette.

segments.speaker: Zach Mack
segments.text: I don't know if that's a joke. I'm not sure.

segments.speaker: Dad
segments.text: It's partially a joke, but it's also real. I mean, it could be--

segments.speaker: Zach Mack
segments.text: It went on like this, all political. Dad's other predictions were that Nancy Pelosi would also be convicted of treason. Same for Bill and Hillary Clinton, who would go down for murder as well. That Trump would be reinstated without an election and cleared of all charges. That Biden would be removed from office. Same for both the governor and mayor of New York. And as a New York City resident, I didn't hate that last one.

segments.speaker: Zach Mack
segments.text: That one, I'm actually kind of hopeful we get that one because I don't really love Eric Adams. He's kind of an idiot. So I'm with you on that one. [CHUCKLES]

segments.speaker: Dad
segments.text: Yep, he's a total idiot. And I'm impressed that you see that. So, good.

segments.speaker: Zach Mack
segments.text: [CHUCKLES]

segments.speaker: Dad
segments.text: One we can both cheer for.

segments.speaker: Zach Mack
segments.text: Eventually, we landed on his final prediction for 2024, his boldest one.

segments.speaker: Dad
segments.text: Number 10-- I threw this in because I thought you'd be excited about it.

segments.speaker: Zach Mack
segments.text: Yeah, it's an exciting one. It's probably the most exciting one.

segments.speaker: Dad
segments.text: The US will come under martial law in 2024 because of mass rioting and chaos. So the military will have to step in.

segments.speaker: Zach Mack
segments.text: For the record, I was never actually excited about the possibility of this happening.

segments.speaker: Zach Mack
segments.text: Do you think this will be happening all over the country, only in certain parts?

segments.speaker: Dad
segments.text: Well, the whole United States will come under martial law. And the biggest cities will be targeted-- New York, unfortunately, Washington DC, the Bay Area.

segments.speaker: Zach Mack
segments.text: OK. You seem pretty confident about that.

segments.speaker: Dad
segments.text: I am 100% confident.

segments.speaker: Zach Mack
segments.text: Because this is a pretty huge shake-up.

segments.speaker: Dad
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Zach Mack
segments.text: I would say, our country hasn't seen anything like this since the Civil War, probably.

segments.speaker: Dad
segments.text: Well, not even in the Civil War. This is going to be the biggest shake-up to ever hit the United States of America and the world at large.

segments.speaker: Zach Mack
segments.text: I mean, I think the way you've laid it out here, there'll be a pretty clear case of, like, who's right and who's wrong.

segments.speaker: Dad
segments.text: Yeah. Yeah. I think it will be very black and white.

segments.speaker: Zach Mack
segments.text: And if you are wrong--

segments.speaker: Dad
segments.text: Then you're $10,000 richer.

segments.speaker: Zach Mack
segments.text: [CHUCKLES] Yeah, but look, this isn't just about the money, right? I would like to make some positive strides for our family.

segments.speaker: Dad
segments.text: Well, I think that once you see that I haven't been duped by AI and social media and the algorithms, I think you will gain a lot more respect for who I am and how I think and how I've come to believe. The other thing I want to have you say after each one of these--

segments.speaker: Zach Mack
segments.text: Uh-huh.

segments.speaker: Dad
segments.text: --too, is that, wow, Dad, you were right, and I was wrong.

segments.speaker: Zach Mack
segments.text: Same goes for you then.

segments.speaker: Dad
segments.text: OK. Absolutely.

segments.speaker: Zach Mack
segments.text: All right. Deal. Happy to do it.

segments.speaker: Dad
segments.text: All right.

segments.speaker: Zach Mack
segments.text: And so our strange bet was on. I saw Dad's challenge as an opening. Instead of just arguing until the end of time, we were actually going to settle this. And now we had a deadline-- New Year's 2025. The moment I saw his proposal, I knew I had him beat.

segments.speaker: Zach Mack
segments.text: And for the very first time, he'd have to admit he was wrong. All I had to do was wait 12 months, and once he decisively lost, I figured he'd be more open to my version of the truth, and maybe I could pull him back to reality a bit. And the timing for the bet couldn't be better because his beliefs were starting to tear our family apart.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Coming up, Zach calls his mom, who has some news of her own. Stay with us.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: This American Life. Zach Mack picks up his story about his year-long bet with his dad.

segments.speaker: Zach Mack
segments.text: Not long after making the bet, I called my mom. My parents have been married for 40 years. They met in their 20s in Chicago, fell in love, and moved to California, where they eventually had my sister and I. We grew up in the San Francisco Bay area, a pretty liberal place, which worked for my mom because she's a pretty liberal Jewish woman.

segments.speaker: Zach Mack
segments.text: Dad has always been the odd man out, the lone Christian conservative, though growing up he was much quieter about his beliefs. And when my parents met, neither of them were religious. But Dad got back into it when I was young. Now he's very into it. That's been difficult for my parents for decades. But now, with the conspiracy stuff emerging, it's been really hard on my mom.

segments.speaker: Mom
segments.text: It's getting pretty crazy, and I don't even know half of it. We have two generators in the house. There are now eight flats of water in the garage that he bought at Costco and some kind of fancy water filter system that was a couple hundred dollars. He's stockpiling weird food.

segments.speaker: Zach Mack
segments.text: What kind of food?

segments.speaker: Mom
segments.text: 12 cans of canned chicken.

segments.speaker: Zach Mack
segments.text: [CHUCKLES] OK.

segments.speaker: Mom
segments.text: And I'm like, I have never eaten canned chicken. You have never eaten canned chicken. Why is there canned chicken? I feel like returning it all this week while he's not home. And he moved some money without my permission.

segments.speaker: Zach Mack
segments.text: How did he do that? He didn't need your sign-off?

segments.speaker: Mom
segments.text: No, because it's a joint account. And he withdrew money from a joint account without telling me and made a purchase he knew I would never approve.

segments.speaker: Zach Mack
segments.text: What was it?

segments.speaker: Mom
segments.text: He bought a precious metal.

segments.speaker: Zach Mack
segments.text: Because Dad's worried the banks are going to collapse, he wants to move big chunks of their money into things like platinum and silver.

segments.speaker: Zach Mack
segments.text: Why is he so unwilling to listen to everyone around him?

segments.speaker: Mom
segments.text: I don't know. I wish I knew because then I could crack it. I don't know how to pull him back. I have been very clear that I'm not sure how much more I can take. And--

segments.speaker: Zach Mack
segments.text: Have you been clear with him about that?

segments.speaker: Mom
segments.text: Yeah, and I've even said, I'm considering leaving, ending the marriage.

segments.speaker: Zach Mack
segments.text: You said that to him?

segments.speaker: Mom
segments.text: Yeah. Which is very hard for me to say, because I'm 69. I'm about to retire.

segments.speaker: Zach Mack
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Mom
segments.text: Not necessarily the life I had planned for myself, to be alone. But what kind of life do I have now?

segments.speaker: Zach Mack
segments.text: Mom was initially irritated by the bet because Dad didn't run it by her first, which happens a lot, but the idea of a deadline, that was starting to make sense to her.

segments.speaker: Mom
segments.text: I need an endpoint. And so the endpoint is December 31. When January 1 comes around, things have to change. I'm only going to put up-- I can barely put up with it now, and I can't put up with it after that.

segments.speaker: Zach Mack
segments.text: Later, I called my sister Kira about the bet. Unfortunately, she's been having her own conflict with Dad, also about his beliefs. Two years ago, Kira came out to him. My mom and I had known for years, but Kira was always afraid to tell Dad because she thought he'd disapprove. It didn't go well. He said he'd always love my sister, but he thought she was choosing to be gay, and he didn't agree with that choice.

segments.speaker: Kira
segments.text: I think the hardest part is that he looked at me and told me that I was wrong about myself, and that he was right. And I don't understand how he could know that.

segments.speaker: Zach Mack
segments.text: Kira and I are close. And when I told her about the bet, she liked the idea of forcing Dad to confront the reality that some of his beliefs are likely wrong. But we weren't sure if that helped her situation either way.

segments.speaker: Kira
segments.text: So, like, let's say these things don't come true, and he's willing to say, like, I was wrong about these things, I don't feel like that would affect his beliefs around me. Like even if he's right about everything else, I'm probably still going to be gay after that.

segments.speaker: Zach Mack
segments.text: So Dad and I had a year. January came and went, and neither of us put any points on the board with the bet. Then in February, Dad caught a small break with Mayor Adams. He had been under investigation for months, and things were heating up. The FBI raided one of his advisors, and someone else pled guilty to conspiracy charges. It seemed like Dad could actually win that one.

segments.speaker: Zach Mack
segments.text: Then in March, the New York governor sent the National Guard into the subway, which, if you squint, could look like the pretense to martial law. While we waited for the other predictions to come true or not, I tried to make the most of the time.

segments.speaker: Zach Mack
segments.text: I found myself thinking back to something Dad said to me at the end of an argument once a few years back. He said, well, you don't really know me. And I wondered if he might be right, that maybe I didn't really know him. And if I had any hope of changing his mind or even nudging the trajectory of his beliefs, I would need to understand my father better.

segments.speaker: Zach Mack
segments.text: So I decided to make a project of it. One question I still had was how he'd even gotten here, though, looking back, there were signs. I remember my mom telling me about how when I was a child, Dad didn't want me to get vaccinated. Mom wasn't having it, so I ended up getting all my shots. But I never really understood where Dad's hangups came from. But now that we had some time to kill, I could ask him.

segments.speaker: Zach Mack
segments.text: I know, throughout my lifetime, you have been distrusting of vaccines. Is that fair to say?

segments.speaker: Dad
segments.text: Yeah. Yeah, that's definitely true.

segments.speaker: Zach Mack
segments.text: I'm wondering when that began.

segments.speaker: Dad
segments.text: Well, the seed was planted, actually, before I went to school.

segments.speaker: Zach Mack
segments.text: As a child?

segments.speaker: Dad
segments.text: As a child.

segments.speaker: Zach Mack
segments.text: Back in the '60s, Dad was about to enter elementary school in Ohio, and there was a new law requiring vaccines.

segments.speaker: Dad
segments.text: Now, remember, Grandpa, my dad, was a chiropractor. And so he believed in natural immunity and the body's ability to heal itself. And so he was an anti-vaxxer.

segments.speaker: Zach Mack
segments.text: OK.

segments.speaker: Dad
segments.text: And I mean, we didn't call him that back then, but it's the same difference. And I just wanted to go to school, and I kept telling my dad and my mom, hey, it's OK, you know? I'm not afraid of the vaccination. I'm willing to go. And I just want to go to school. So I was not able to go to kindergarten because we couldn't find a school that would accept me without a vaccination.

segments.speaker: Zach Mack
segments.text: Oh, wow. So you didn't go to kindergarten?

segments.speaker: Dad
segments.text: I did not go to kindergarten.

segments.speaker: Zach Mack
segments.text: Well, do you think your dad was-- I don't know. How would you describe him? Would you describe him as stubborn?

segments.speaker: Dad
segments.text: Oh, yeah. Stubborn, very opinionated, hard-headed at times.

segments.speaker: Zach Mack
segments.text: Dad was one of six children. The family was supported primarily by my grandpa, who had a small chiropractic business. That is, until the Ohio State Medical Board cracked down on him.

segments.speaker: Dad
segments.text: And so they literally threw my dad in jail for a couple of days--

segments.speaker: Zach Mack
segments.text: Wow.

segments.speaker: Dad
segments.text: --for practicing without a license.

segments.speaker: Zach Mack
segments.text: The way Dad tells it, after my grandfather's business dissolved, he was never able to recover. He became so depressed that he literally couldn't get out of bed for, like, six months. And he was never the same man. That literally broke him.

segments.speaker: Zach Mack
segments.text: Wow. And how old were you when this happened?

segments.speaker: Dad
segments.text: I was, like, 13 or 14 years old.

segments.speaker: Zach Mack
segments.text: One of the things I remember most about my grandfather is how tall and thin he was, and how, one time when he came to visit us, his body had just completely changed. He had suddenly gained over 100 pounds in a very short amount of time. He was going through some mental health issues that the family never fully understood, and it was affecting his weight and his ability to sleep.

segments.speaker: Zach Mack
segments.text: He wouldn't really sleep during the night, which meant that throughout the day, he would constantly fall asleep. He'd be in the middle of a conversation sometimes, or even at dinner, and he'd just start snoring. Minutes later, he'd abruptly wake up and carry on as if nothing happened.

segments.speaker: Zach Mack
segments.text: This also began to happen while he was driving. My grandpa got into a number of car accidents. He totaled several cars and nearly killed my grandmother. He refused to stop driving and even went to a neighboring state to get a driver's license after his was taken away. He refused to admit anything was wrong.

segments.speaker: Zach Mack
segments.text: The family tried to talk to him. So did my father several times. And when that didn't work-- and I'd never heard this part of the story before-- Dad tried something else.

segments.speaker: Dad
segments.text: I wrote him a long letter. I wrote him, like, a two or three-page letter and mailed it to him, because I wanted him to be able to read the whole letter so I could finish what I really wanted to say to him without interruption.

segments.speaker: Dad
segments.text: And I said, Dad, I love you. I want the best for you. I'm not trying to say anything horrible or damaging or critical about you, but your whole family is concerned about you. Can't you see this? Can't you recognize that we all would like to see you live to a ripe old age? Because, I said, if you continue on this path, I don't know when you're going to die, but I know you're going to die. So.

segments.speaker: Zach Mack
segments.text: Not long after this-- I was 10 years old at the time-- my parents called my sister and me into the kitchen to tell us something. But before they said anything, I already knew. My grandfather was dead. His vehicle veered off the road and flipped over.

segments.speaker: Zach Mack
segments.text: When I think about my grandfather, I think about how what caused his death may have been stubbornness, a refusal to listen to those around him. He was 68 years old, the same age my father was when he proposed our bet.

segments.speaker: Zach Mack
segments.text: As the year pressed on, we continued discussing Dad's life and the things he'd come to believe. Turns out, a lot of his predictions were coming from a single source online. And something you should know about my father is that he really struggles with technology. He can barely navigate the internet. He can't even figure out how to access his own email account from his laptop.

segments.speaker: Zach Mack
segments.text: Around 2019, Dad got an iPad, and that felt like a turning point. It wasn't long until he started saying weird things. One time, I was home visiting, and we got into it because he was trying to tell me that the government was controlling Facebook from the very beginning, and that Mark Zuckerberg was just a pawn. And when the pandemic hit, it felt like the perfect storm. Like so many of us, Dad went searching for answers.

segments.speaker: Dad
segments.text: I was googling around trying to find someone who I thought was reputable, reliable, and truly plugged into God. I was trying to find someone who was a legitimate prophet, because there's a lot of false prophets out there.

segments.speaker: Zach Mack
segments.text: What Dad found was a lot of conspiracies, of course, but also the next evolution of his faith. During the pandemic, Dad came to believe strongly in prophecy, the idea that God still speaks through intermediaries.

segments.speaker: Zach Mack
segments.text: When you're talking about how God speaks today and you believe it's through prophets, that is a divisive within Christianity, right? That is a divisive thought?

segments.speaker: Dad
segments.text: Very divisive.

segments.speaker: Zach Mack
segments.text: Why do you believe it?

segments.speaker: Dad
segments.text: Because he's always had prophets. And it makes sense that just like he had profits in Old Testament times, he would continue with it. Why would he suddenly stop? I never quite understood why God would stop talking to his people.

segments.speaker: Zach Mack
segments.text: Sure enough, Dad found someone he believes can commune directly with God.

segments.speaker: Julie Green
segments.text: I am the great revealer.

segments.speaker: Zach Mack
segments.text: Meet Julie Green, my dad's preferred prophet.

segments.speaker: Julie Green
segments.text: A great fall is coming, a fall of a global cabal. My children, 2024 will be a year like no other.

segments.speaker: Dad
segments.text: I firmly believe that God did lead me to Julie Green.

segments.speaker: Zach Mack
segments.text: She's not particularly big online, a couple 100,000 subscribers, but she's part of a growing movement within Christianity that emphasizes spiritual warfare and politics. It's all very Trumpy and full of prophecies.

segments.speaker: Julie Green
segments.text: Secrets in the White House are about to be revealed. The Obamas, the Clintons, Adam Schiff, Mitch McConnell, Chuck Schumer, Nancy Pelosi--

segments.speaker: Zach Mack
segments.text: As you can probably tell, this is where Dad's getting most of his predictions. And when I talk to Dad about these predictions, it's clear that for him, they all stem from his religious beliefs, which I've always found somewhat confusing because when I look at his list, none of these things seem to have anything to do with God at all.

segments.speaker: Zach Mack
segments.text: In July, some news-- President Biden announced he was withdrawing as the Democratic nominee for president. I thought, what was Dad's prediction again? Oh, he said, removed from office. Guess I'm in the clear.

segments.speaker: Zach Mack
segments.text: As the year sped by, I read books with titles like When Prophecy Fails. I spoke to a number of clinicians and conspiracy experts, met my dad's pastors. I even interviewed several of his friends. None of them shared his beliefs, but they said they didn't really argue with him about it either. Only one said it hurt their friendship with Dad.

segments.speaker: Zach Mack
segments.text: Sometimes I'd send Dad highlights of articles debunking some of his more out-there claims, like the one about how the Joe Biden you see on the news is actually a body double.

segments.speaker: Dad
segments.text: Well, it's actually a common practice in a lot of third world countries. Look at Saddam Hussein. Saddam Hussein had-- they aren't even sure, but over a half a dozen body doubles. That's why he could appear in one part of the country one day and someplace else another day.

segments.speaker: Zach Mack
segments.text: Yeah, I don't think they were giving speeches and making policy on his behalf, though. You know what I'm saying?

segments.speaker: Dad
segments.text: Some of them were.

segments.speaker: Zach Mack
segments.text: I think they were just maybe like--

segments.speaker: Dad
segments.text: Some of them were.

segments.speaker: Zach Mack
segments.text: --a little quick appearance.

segments.speaker: Dad
segments.text: But mostly, yeah, they were just appearances. Fun fact, while we're talking about body doubles, when the Biden--

segments.speaker: Zach Mack
segments.text: Why do you call him "the Biden"?

segments.speaker: Dad
segments.text: Well, because it's a body double.

segments.speaker: Zach Mack
segments.text: [CHUCKLES] OK.

segments.speaker: Dad
segments.text: The last time Netanyahu, who's the Israeli prime minister, came to visit the US here in Washington, DC, it was interesting that the fake Biden stood 6 inches taller than Netanyahu. Netanyahu and Biden are both listed to be 5 feet, 10 inches tall. So don't you find it interesting that when they were standing side by side in a couple of photos, that Biden was suddenly 6 inches taller?

segments.speaker: Zach Mack
segments.text: Well, first of all, Biden's listed height is 6 feet. Let's see what Netanyahu's height is. He's also 6 feet, it says.

segments.speaker: Dad
segments.text: OK, yeah, they're the same height. The point is, they're the same height. I thought it was 5' 10". So yeah. So it's 6 feet.

segments.speaker: Zach Mack
segments.text: Are you talking about this image?

segments.speaker: Dad
segments.text: Yeah, I think that's it. Yeah.

segments.speaker: Zach Mack

segments.speaker: Zach Mack
segments.text: --I took him to go see Ohio State, our favorite football team, play in the Rose Bowl--

segments.speaker: Zach Mack
segments.text: What do you think the score is going to be?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: --and paid for everything.

segments.speaker: Dad
segments.text: I think it's going to be 31 to 22, Bucks.

segments.speaker: Zach Mack
segments.text: Yet another prediction my father got wrong, by the way. But they did win. Go, Buckeyes.

segments.speaker: Dad
segments.text: Let's go! All right! Let's go!

segments.speaker: Zach Mack
segments.text: It felt good to treat dad with his own money and to agree on the one reality we've always shared-- football-- maybe the only one we ever will. As I watched the clock run down, I knew that the moment the game was over, we'd have to face the fact that, as a family, in the end, we didn't make it.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Zach Mack. He's a producer at Vox Media. His story was a collaboration with NPR's Embedded podcast, which, if you haven't heard them, you should check them out. They have lots of documentary stories like this. David Kestenbaum, on our staff, worked on the story here. The staff who worked on it there were producers Dan Girma and Ariana Gharib Lee.

segments.text: Editing by Luis Trelles. Katie Simon is Embedded's showrunner. Some original music in this episode was composed by Peter Leonard. Fact-checking by Gretta Pittenger on the Embedded staff and Christopher Swetala on our staff.

segments.text: NPR's Embedded is releasing a three-part series about Zach's bet with his dad that gets into material that we did not have time for here, including some revealing conversations with his dad's friends and some more interesting stuff from Zach and his dad.
